question: Summarize what the Python debugging playbook says about scope errors.
answer: The Python Debugging Playbook on scope errors states that UnboundLocalError occurs when a function assigns to a name and then reads it before the assignment runs. [S1] Fixes include passing the value as a parameter, using the global statement, or using the nonlocal statement to bind a name from the nearest enclosing function scope. [S1] The fix for the late-binding closure issue is to bind the value from the loop variable using nonlocal. [S1]

citations.title: Python Debugging Playbook
citations.text:
2. Scope Errors
UnboundLocalError (message: local variable referenced before assignment) happens when a
function assigns to a name anywhere in its body, which makes that name local for the entire
function, and then reads the name before the assignment has run. The usual symptom is code that
works at module level but fails once it is moved inside a function.
Three fixes exist. Pass the value in as a parameter, which is the cleanest option. Use the global
statement to bind a module-level name. Use the nonlocal statement to bind a name from the
nearest enclosing function scope; nonlocal cannot reach module-level names.
A related surprise is the late-binding closure: lambdas created in a loop all see the final value of the
loop variable. The fix is to bind the current value through a default argument, for example lambda
i=i: i.

S2.title: Python Debugging Playbook
S2.text:
1. Reading a Traceback
A traceback lists the chain of calls that led to an error. Read it from the bottom: the last line names
the exception type and its message, and the frames above it show the call chain with the most
recent call last. Start with the last frame inside your own code, because frames inside library code
are rarely the cause.
The built-in breakpoint() pauses execution and opens the debugger pdb by default (since Python
3.7). You can also start a script under the debugger with python -m pdb script.py. Inside pdb the
command n runs the next line, s steps into a call, c continues until the next breakpoint, p expr prints
an expression and q quits.
Print debugging still works: print(repr(value)) is more informative than print(value) because repr
shows quotes, escape characters and trailing spaces.

S3.title: Python Reference Notes
S3.text:
COMMON ERRORS AND THEIR MEANING
SyntaxError: the code is not valid Python, for example a missing colon after if.
IndentationError: the indentation of a block is inconsistent.
NameError: a variable or function name was used before it was defined.
TypeError: an operation was applied to the wrong type, such as "a" + 1.
ValueError: the type is right but the value is not, such as int("abc").
KeyError: a dictionary key does not exist.
IndexError: a list index is outside the valid range.
ZeroDivisionError: division or modulo by zero.
FileNotFoundError: the file path does not exist.

S4.title: Python Debugging Playbook
S4.text:
3. Lookup Errors Compared
KeyError is raised when a dictionary key is missing. IndexError is raised when a sequence index is
out of range. AttributeError is raised when an object has no attribute of that name.
The message 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'append' almost always means a variable holds
None instead of a list. The classic cause is writing nums = nums.sort(), because list.sort() sorts in
place and returns None. Use nums.sort() on its own line or sorted(nums) when a new list is
needed.
dict.get(key, default) avoids a KeyError, while collections.defaultdict(list) creates a missing key with
an empty list the first time it is accessed, which makes grouping code shorter.
